How OpenAI delivers low-latency voice AI at scale
Articles
·
OpenAI Blog
·
Yesterday

This engineering blog post from OpenAI details the architectural redesign of their WebRTC infrastructure to support low-latency voice AI for over 900 million weekly active users. The core challenge was running WebRTC, a stateful protocol requiring one UDP port per session, on Kubernetes, which is designed for stateless, elastic workloads. The team solved this by splitting the WebRTC stack into two components: a lightweight, stateless relay that handles packet routing and a stateful transceiver that terminates the WebRTC protocol. The relay uses the ICE username fragment (ufrag) embedded in STUN packets to deterministically route the first packet to the correct transceiver, eliminating the need for large, dynamic UDP port ranges. This design, combined with a global relay layer for geo-steering, reduces first-hop latency and jitter. The post details the trade-offs between SFU and transceiver architectures, the implementation of the relay in Go with optimizations like SO_REUSEPORT and thread pinning, and the key learnings from the project, emphasizing the principle of adding complexity in a thin routing layer rather than in backend services.

Marcus Moretti, general manager of Spiral, describes how he uses Claude Code to run product management as a solo practitioner. He explains that the only document he writes himself is the roadmap; Claude generates all PRDs and tickets from it. He uses a custom `/pulse` command for daily analytics that reads user conversations and flags anomalies, replacing traditional dashboards. For research, Claude helps him navigate academic literature via an Arxiv MCP. He argues that AI tools make true Agile possible and that SaaS products can survive by owning unique data sources and offering seamless agent integrations. The essay emphasizes that AI removes busywork, allowing PMs to focus on strategy, user research, and creative problem-solving.

The article argues that the dominant paradigm of AI agents as single-session chat loops has hit a ceiling, and the next frontier is long-running agents that can operate over hours, days, or weeks. It identifies three fundamental walls: finite context windows, lack of persistent state across sessions, and the inability of models to reliably self-verify. The author then presents a detailed survey of how major players are solving these problems. Anthropic's approach is detailed through its harness designs and the 'brain/hands/session' decoupling in Managed Agents. Cursor's solution involves a planner/worker/judge architecture, with different models assigned to different roles. Google's Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform productizes these patterns with services like Agent Runtime, Agent Sessions, and Memory Bank. The article distills five production design patterns (checkpoint-and-resume, delegated approval, memory-layered context, ambient processing, fleet orchestration) and provides practical advice for developers, product builders, and those creating autonomous operational agents. It concludes by acknowledging current limitations like cost, security, and alignment drift, and predicts the next hard problems will be in multi-agent coordination.

This article announces a new protocol co-designed by Cloudflare and Stripe, launched as part of Stripe Projects, that allows AI coding agents to autonomously provision cloud infrastructure. Agents can now create a Cloudflare account, start a paid subscription, register a domain, and obtain an API token to deploy code, all without a human needing to visit a dashboard or enter payment details. The protocol is built on three core components: Discovery (a catalog of available services agents can query), Authorization (Stripe acts as an identity provider, allowing Cloudflare to automatically create accounts or link existing ones via OAuth), and Payment (Stripe provides a payment token, with a default $100/month spending limit, so agents never handle raw credit card data). The article details the end-to-end flow using the Stripe Projects CLI, explains how the protocol works under the hood, and emphasizes that any platform with signed-in users can integrate with Cloudflare in the same way Stripe does, treating agents as a first-class concern. This standardizes cross-product integrations that were previously bespoke and one-off.

This presentation transcript by Jimmy Morzaria, a Staff Software Engineer at Stripe, provides a deep dive into the architecture and engineering behind Stripe's internal document database service, DocDB. The talk begins by framing the challenge: Stripe processes trillions of dollars in payments with 5.5 nines of reliability, requiring a database infrastructure that handles over 5 million queries per second across petabytes of data. The core of the solution is a zero-downtime data movement platform built on top of open-source MongoDB. The article explains the step-by-step process of migrating data chunks between shards, including bulk importing sorted data for 10x throughput gains, bidirectional asynchronous replication for fast rollback, and a custom version-gating protocol to orchestrate traffic switches in milliseconds. Beyond horizontal scaling, the platform is also used for database version upgrades and migrating between single-tenant and multi-tenant architectures. The talk concludes with key takeaways on the importance of reliability, investing in strong foundational infrastructure, and a framework for deciding whether to build or buy a capability.

The DPoP Storage Paradox: Why Browser-Based Proof-of-Possession Remains an Unsolved Problem
Articles
·
InfoQ
·
04-30
92

The article examines a critical security gap in browser-based DPoP (RFC 9449) implementations: while the protocol binds tokens to client key pairs, it leaves key storage unspecified. The author demonstrates that storing private keys as non-extractable CryptoKeys in IndexedDB does not prevent XSS exploitation, as attackers can invoke `crypto.subtle.sign()` to forge DPoP proofs without extracting the key. This 'Oracle Attack' is documented in the IETF's own security considerations. The article evaluates the Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) pattern as the current industry standard, which moves key material server-side and prevents both the Oracle Attack and fresh token acquisition attacks. For deployments where a BFF is infeasible (e.g., browser extensions, embedded widgets), the author presents a memory-only key approach with a Lazy Re-Binding handshake, which limits the XSS blast radius to a single session. The article concludes by comparing these patterns and discussing future directions like Device Bound Session Credentials (DBSC).

This article is a transcript of a speech by Zhang Zehua, Algorithm Director at JD.com Group, at AICon 2025. It systematically elaborates on JD.com's practical approach to transitioning from traditional CTR models to generative large models in the advertising recommendation domain. The core is the GRAM architecture, which uses a deep reasoning mechanism to achieve direct semantic alignment between user intent and SKUs, and employs fast and slow dual-pathways to handle quick clicks and complex decisions respectively. On the engineering front, the article details how techniques like PD separation, probability space pruning, and multi-level caching stabilize inference latency within 50ms. Furthermore, the article highlights the evolution from feature engineering to knowledge engineering, systematizing retail experience into twelve major knowledge categories, building a deep cascading knowledge graph for real-time queries within 5ms, and effectively suppressing hallucinations. The article also discusses challenges of generative models in advertising, including hallucination, lack of controllability, and difficulty in ROI validation, proposing a solution path with rule-based systems as a safety net and human-machine collaboration. Finally, it recommends a phased advancement strategy, gradually transitioning from general models to domain-specific knowledge-enhanced models.
